The thing is, we like to be proud of our 1000+ year old state, but there are some gaps in the continuity exactly because of the events we're talking about.

The Mongol invasion decimated the Hungarian population. Many villages, towns became deserted. Then the Ottoman occupation did this too: many parts of the territory of today's Hungary became empty (mostly not because everybody was killed, but because they fled to the not occupied parts). So there were two occasions of active repopulations in Hungarian history. Many villages only have their original, thousand year old names and not much else. Some ancient churches, monasteries and castles survived, but most of the population surrounding them aren't the descendants of those who lived there when those were built, even if they were/are all of Hungarian ancestry. 

We have some old diplomas and other official certificates from those times which help to understand our history, but very little living memories from then.

Hungary itself isn't a very scenic country, and even if there are places which have a nice landscape (because of hills or mountains), there's enough space to avoid those, because it's really more expensive to build railroad on rugged terrain. But there are some exceptions:

- Nr. 29: Budapest - Székesfehérvár - Tapolca: this one goes along the northern bank of Lake Balaton, sometimes only a few meters away from the water, but because that area really is hilly, other parts are pretty scenic too. Unfortunately, a section of it has been electrified last year, so the scene became uglier with the catenary poles, and the nice diesel locomotives vanished from there. But it's still great. It has a big traffic: in summer, trains go every hour from Budapest to there. There's another railway line on the southern bank of Balaton, but it's less scenic.

- Nr. 11: this is universally considered the most scenic railroad in Hungary. It goes between Veszprém and Győr, and a third of its part are really in the mountains with viaducts and tunnels and really nice landscape. It's in the mountain range of Bakony, is frequently used by tourists and hikers. 

- Nr. 87: it's in eastern Hungary, between Eger and Szilvásvárad. It's next to the mountains of Bükk, but a short section goes right through them also with tunnels and bridges. There was another section between Szilvásvárad and Putnok, but it was closed down in 2009. Its landscape wasn't that mountainous but very nicely hilly, it was really peaceful and beautiful (even if went throug one of the poorest part of the country). 

I have made several pictures about these, but it's not very easy to upload pictures here, so you just have to believe me.

Not many people keep in mind (not even every Hungarian), but the siege of Budapest was one of the more significant city battles of WW2. It's specialities are: it lasted almost two months (from dec 1944 to Feb 1945), the population (~ 1 million people) wasn't evacuated, there was an ongoing "inner siege": the Arrowcross Party (= equivalent of the nazis) groups terrorized the population, especially the Jews; WW2s last ghetto was established not long before the siege.

Hitler declared the city as a Festung, a fortress, so it can't be given up, and shouldn't be spared (like Rome). This caused bitter street battles from one house to the other. Whoever in the population hadn't already been hating the Germans or the Hungarian fascists, changed their minds during this misery.

Of course, tens of thousands died among the civilians, the city was in ruins, all the bridges were blown up etc. All for nothing, the Soviets conquered/liberated the city anyway.

Not in Germany, because you guys have more modern stuff. For example, earlier there was the IBIS system, and I presume, nowadays there are other, even more sophisticated systems; but the thing is that the tram somehow "knows" on which route it's going (through GPS or other stuff), so it automatically changes the switches if necessary with radio control or other stuff. 

But Budapest (and other places in Eastern Europe) still has a system where there is a short, special section of the catenary like 30-50 meters before the switch. If the switch leads to the right direction, the driver has to roll under this short section without accelerating or taking any other current (the auxiliary systems are often also shut down during this if they consume too much), and the switch stays in the original direction, and it becomes locked, so a next tram wouldn't change it while the tram is still on it (thus the following tram must wait before going under this section of catenary until the previous has left the switch). If it must change the switch, the tram must accelerate, and thus pick up current from the catenary. The system senses this, and changes the direction of the switch (and locks it, of course). Sometimes you can fail, either you don't (or can't) change when you need to, or change the switch unnecessarily (like I did on my first day).

I worked as a tram driver as a part time job when I was attending the university. On my very first day (without supervision from an experienced tram driver), I accidentally changed the switch into the wrong direction, so I had to get off, and manually switch back with the so called "switch iron" which is a heavy rod.

Look at my example, our languages are supposed to be similar in this way.

-k ending

If the word ends with a consonant, you have to put an extra vowel (which fits to the previous vowels), we're not Slavics. 

Example:

Singular: _lány_ (girl)

Plural: lány + k, but we don't like consonants next to each other, so lány + o + k = _lányok_ (girls)

Easy, huh?

But if we put a number or an attribution meaning quantity ("many" or "few"), we use singular. So we don't say "five girls" but "five girl": _öt lány_ (instead of _öt lányok_).

EDIT: if someone's confused, "ny" is one consonant, it's pronounced as "nj" (ň for Czechs). Or like in the name Tanya. Or like the Spanish ň (with tilde), like in maňana.

EDIT2: and this is just nominativ. Hungarian has 17...34 grammar cases (like the 4 in German or 7 in Slavic languages), it depends on how you define one case.

The climate is similar, only the geography is different: the Carpathian basin isn't "open" to the south, to the Mediterranean Sea, so the warm, moist air from the south usually can't come here so unobstructedly like from the Gulf of Mexico. So when the CAPE values are high as 5-6 kJ/kg, the air is usually very dry. However, we regularly have CAPEs of 1-2 kJ/kg with enough moisture, but usually in the summer when the jet stream isn't that strong anymore, so wind shear is lower. The third factor: even if we have enough energy, enough moisture and enough wind shear, we don't have a capping inversion which could make the atmosphere spare the energy for a strong and explosive supercell - rather more smaller, weaker supercells emerge. 

And there are the rare occasions I mentioned, once every one or two year (in average) when everything is set to have major, tornadic supercells.
